body_markdown:
There’s a lot to say when sending your youngest child off to college after enjoying 18 years of his company. And while that time has come for me, mercifully, for you, I won’t say all these things here. Just to report, we packed young Milo Kitman off to school in Washington, D.C. last month, and to say it was bittersweet would be an understatement. For reasons unknown, he is the most agreeable Kitman I’ve ever met, reasonable, open-minded, and even-tempered with rarely an unkind word for anyone. Where, one might wonder, did this lad come from?


In July, when we attended a two-day orientation program at his new school we took the Amtrak to D.C., which I always enjoy. But this time, with things to move into a dorm room, we had to drive and, while an old Rover SD1—a capacious load hauler—might have cut it, it might not have. Today was not the day to find out: A brand-new Ford Explorer from Ford’s press fleet arrived and filled the bill nicely.


[Jamie Kitman](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/jkitman/)


I’m not going to lie. The SUV-ification of America (and, to be fair, large parts of the whole world) is not a trend that I’ve endorsed historically and I’m not likely to change my mind. I come from a time when the enthusiast virtues most celebrated were lively handling, roadholding, beauty, and, wherever possible, fuel economy. All of which benefited from machines no bigger or heavier than they had to be.


Thirty-two years ago, I even wrote what I believe to have been America’s first-ever anti-SUV op-ed piece for the *New York Times* . Mind you, I didn’t say there shouldn’t be any SUVs—the libertarian streak in me says people ought to drive what they want (I know I do) but I felt compelled to point out that those city dwellers who thought they were safer in SUVs (they manifestly weren’t then, and the statistics proved it)—or somehow signified their exceptional one-ness with the Earth—were sadly mistaken. What they were was more profitable for their makers. Like decades of cars ever lower, longer, and wider, even today, half a century on, taller, longer, and wider equals higher transaction prices and bigger profits. Same idea.


For the industry, the math proved addictive. And, for better or worse, no one was listening to me—or other critics—anyway. The good news was that, gradually, SUVs became safer and more fuel-efficient than ever, with the added bonus that they handled better and were more fun to drive. Safer and less scary, too.


Scary how, you ask? I still remember the afternoon of December 29, 1988, when as a young car tester I drove a Ford Bronco II down to Philadelphia for a They Might Be Giants’ show at the city’s Theater of the Living Arts—a venue which, unlike the Bronco II, is still with us. The small two-door SUV based on the then-current Ford Ranger pickup had to be discontinued owing to rollover concerns, which did not surprise me. Even in that far-away time, I remember thinking that the Bronco II felt about as stable on the highway as a Jenga game during a major seismic event. Speaking of rollovers, its replacement, the original Ford Explorer, while improved and much better-selling, didn’t fare much better. It left Ford with a multi-billion black eye when it emerged that low tire pressures, combined with heavy loads and bad driving (a human constant, sad to say), endowed their smash hit with an unwelcome propensity for… rolling over.


Jamie Kitman


Not so the 2026 Explorer that Milo and I took to Washington, D.C. Its road manners on a 450-mile round trip were exemplary. Riding and handling nicely, it was an actual pleasure to drive, belying its height and approximate 4800 pounds of weight, which nowadays makes it just mid-size. The SUV easily swallowed eight duffle bags of clothing and electronic equipment and could’ve easily held more. It probably would have if the dorm rooms weren’t so small. Just as impressive was the new Explorer’s bright and airy interior whose quality plastics and fabrics will forever (we hope) banish memories of old Explorers and their riots of cheap plastic, vinyl, and ersatz wood to the dustbin of history. Even my wife and Milo (who is not a gearhead) were moved to comment on how pleasant the cabin was. Kudos, Ford.


Jamie Kitman


Jamie Kitman


College man installed—and I know he’s attending classes, because he dropped the word “existentialism” into a telephone call the other day—I returned home that same day from the District of Columbia alone, my mind and heart filled with contradictory thoughts and feelings. Happy to see the boy grown up and doing so well. Sad to see him go. Distracted by these emotions while filling up with regular gasoline for the journey back to New York, I nearly missed that the Explorer had somehow managed 26 miles per gallon. Considering the high price of gas these days, the size of the vehicle and the high speeds our early morning start permitted, the figure amazed me. The Explorer repeated the feat on the journey home.


Jamie Kitman


More sophisticated engine management gets part of the credit, but perhaps even more so, thanks for squeezing that many miles out of a tank go to the Explorer’s 10-speed automatic transmission. Reminding us that, despite all the denials and corporate hand-wringing, better gas mileage may have always been within reach were more gears added to the equation. While one may then ponder why it took so long for carmakers to come around to this way of thinking, whether it was some sort of epiphany or they knew it all along and were just too cost-averse to specify the fuel-saving additional cogs, we may never know. But at least we’ve made it this far, with a little prodding from Uncle Sam. I’m glad that automakers are putting what they’ve learned to good use and, like I’ve advised my last college student, aren’t cutting corners for short-term gain. Long may you both run.


***


*A man of many pursuits (rock band manager, automotive journalist, concours judge, purveyor of picture cars for film and TV), Jamie Kitman lives and breathes vintage machines.
